blocks.content: Think about a small restaurant with one kitchen. The same kitchen cooks the starters, the mains, and the desserts. One set of pots, one set of staff, one door in and out. Nobody is calling a separate building to get the soup made.
That kitchen is a monolith. Everything lives and runs together, and for a small restaurant that is not a bad thing at all, it is actually the easiest way to run a kitchen.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260797-721659280.png
blocks.alt: Catalog, cart, and orders modules all running inside one process

blocks.content: 1. Introduction

A monolithic architecture means your entire application, every module, every feature, ships as one deployable unit. One codebase, one build, one deploy, and usually one database sitting behind all of it. There is no separate service for users, another for orders, and another for payments. It is all one program.

This is not an old fashioned mistake that only legacy systems make. Most successful products, including plenty of famous ones, started this way and stayed this way for years. Understanding why monoliths work, and where they eventually strain, is one of the most practical things you can know walking into a system design interview.
1.1 What actually counts as a monolith
blocks.text: 1.1 What actually counts as a monolith

blocks.content: The word gets thrown around loosely, so it helps to be precise. A monolith is defined by deployment, not by how messy or clean the code inside it is.

["One codebase all the source code for every feature lives in a single repository, or at least builds into a single artifact.","One build compiling or bundling the app produces a single output, not a dozen separate outputs.","One deploy shipping a change means deploying that one artifact, there is nothing to deploy independently.","Usually one database most monoliths lean on a single shared database, since there is no hard boundary forcing data apart."]
items: One codebase all the source code for every feature lives in a single repository, or at least builds into a single artifact.
One build compiling or bundling the app produces a single output, not a dozen separate outputs.
One deploy shipping a change means deploying that one artifact, there is nothing to deploy independently.
Usually one database most monoliths lean on a single shared database, since there is no hard boundary forcing data apart.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260799-221355490.png
blocks.alt: The whole monolith reading and writing to a single shared database

blocks.content: 2. Why monoliths are a genuinely good starting point
blocks.text: 2. Why monoliths are a genuinely good starting point

blocks.content: It is easy to hear "monolith" and assume it means outdated or naive. In reality, a monolith removes a huge pile of problems that only show up once you split an app into separate services. Early on, those problems are not worth paying for.
2.1 Simplicity you can hold in your head
blocks.text: 2.1 Simplicity you can hold in your head

blocks.content: With one codebase, there is one place to look for anything. You do not need a map of which service owns which feature, or a diagram just to remember how requests flow between processes. New engineers can clone one repository, run one command, and see the whole system working on their laptop.
2.2 No network calls between your own modules
blocks.text: 2.2 No network calls between your own modules

blocks.content: When the cart module needs something from the catalog module, that is a plain function call inside the same process. No HTTP request, no serialization, no retry logic, no worrying about the network being slow or down. It just runs.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260800-346027833.png
blocks.alt: A function call between modules staying inside the same process, no network hop

blocks.title: This is the biggest hidden cost of microservices
blocks.content: The moment you split modules into separate services, every one of those in process function calls turns into a network call, with all the latency and failure modes that come with it. A monolith sidesteps that entirely.
2.3 Transactions are straightforward

Placing an order might need to update inventory, create an order record, and charge a cart total, all at once, all or nothing. Inside one database, that is a normal database transaction. Across separate services with separate databases, you would need distributed transactions or sagas, both of which are genuinely hard to get right.
2.4 Debugging is easier

When something breaks, you have one process, one log stream, and one stack trace to look at. You are not hopping across five different services trying to piece together what happened to a single request. A single debugger session can step through the entire flow.

3. Where the downsides actually show up
blocks.text: 3. Where the downsides actually show up

blocks.content: None of this means monoliths are free forever. As the app, the team, and the traffic grow, some real cracks start to appear. It helps to know exactly what those cracks look like, rather than treating "monoliths do not scale" as a vague slogan.
3.1 The whole app scales together

Say your catalog module gets hammered by traffic during a big sale, while cart and orders stay quiet. In a monolith, you cannot scale just the catalog code. Scaling means running more copies of the entire process, cart and orders included, even though they are not the bottleneck. You are paying to scale code that does not need it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260800-190760769.png
blocks.alt: One hot module forcing the whole monolith to scale together

blocks.content: 3.2 One team can break another team's feature
blocks.text: 3.2 One team can break another team's feature

blocks.content: When everyone commits to the same codebase, a change meant for the orders module can accidentally break something in cart, especially if they share code or a database schema. There is no hard wall stopping one team's mistake from leaking into someone else's feature.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260801-829117982.png
blocks.alt: Two teams shipping into the same codebase and one change breaking an unrelated feature

blocks.content: 3.3 Deploys get scarier as the codebase grows
blocks.text: 3.3 Deploys get scarier as the codebase grows

blocks.content: Deploying a monolith means deploying everything at once. A tiny fix to how prices are rounded ships alongside every other change sitting in that release, whether it was tested well or not. The bigger the codebase and the more people committing to it, the more nervous a deploy tends to feel.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260801-84153168.png
blocks.alt: Deploy risk climbing as the codebase grows larger

blocks.content: 3.4 A crash anywhere is a crash everywhere
blocks.text: 3.4 A crash anywhere is a crash everywhere

blocks.content: Since every module runs inside the same process, an unhandled exception or a memory leak in one module can take the whole application down. The orders module misbehaving does not just break checkout, it can crash catalog browsing too, because they were never actually isolated from each other.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260801-307816334.png
blocks.alt: A bug in the orders module crashing catalog and cart along with it

blocks.title: This is a fault isolation problem, not a scaling problem
blocks.content: Splitting into services fixes this specific issue by putting a process boundary between modules. But that fix brings its own costs, which is exactly why the decision is a trade-off and not a free upgrade.
4. The modular monolith: a middle ground
blocks.text: 4. The modular monolith: a middle ground

blocks.content: You do not have to choose between a tangled ball of code and a fleet of microservices. A modular monolith keeps everything in one deployable unit, but organizes the code internally into modules with real boundaries, almost like each module is a mini service that just happens to run in the same process.
4.1 What makes it modular

["Each module owns its own folder, its own internal logic, and ideally its own set of database tables.","Modules talk to each other through clear interfaces, not by reaching into each other's internals.","A linter or build rule can enforce that catalog code never directly imports cart's internal files.","The whole thing still builds and deploys as one single artifact."]
items: Each module owns its own folder, its own internal logic, and ideally its own set of database tables.
Modules talk to each other through clear interfaces, not by reaching into each other's internals.
A linter or build rule can enforce that catalog code never directly imports cart's internal files.
The whole thing still builds and deploys as one single artifact.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260802-180239732.png
blocks.alt: One deployable unit internally organized into catalog, cart, and orders modules

blocks.content: 4.2 Why bother if it still deploys as one thing
blocks.text: 4.2 Why bother if it still deploys as one thing

blocks.content: Because most of the pain of a messy monolith comes from tangled code, not from the deployment model itself. A modular monolith gets you clean boundaries, easier reasoning, and a much smoother path to splitting a module into its own service later, if that day ever actually comes, all while keeping today's deploys and debugging simple.

blocks.title: Boundaries first, network calls later
blocks.content: If you cannot draw clean lines between your modules while they still live in one process, splitting them into separate services will not fix that, it will just make the same mess slower and harder to debug.
5. When a monolith is the right call, and when it starts to hurt
blocks.text: 5. When a monolith is the right call, and when it starts to hurt

blocks.content: This is a judgment call, not a fixed rule, but there are some patterns that show up again and again.
5.1 When a monolith is genuinely the right choice
blocks.text: 5.1 When a monolith is genuinely the right choice

blocks.content: ["Most startups and early products, where speed of shipping matters more than perfect structure.","Small teams, where the overhead of coordinating across separate services outweighs any benefit.","Unclear domain boundaries, when you genuinely do not know yet where cart ends and orders begins.","Anything where the team is small enough to fit around one table and understand the whole system."]
items: Most startups and early products, where speed of shipping matters more than perfect structure.
Small teams, where the overhead of coordinating across separate services outweighs any benefit.
Unclear domain boundaries, when you genuinely do not know yet where cart ends and orders begins.
Anything where the team is small enough to fit around one table and understand the whole system.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260802-695717314.png
blocks.alt: Small team, unclear domains, and need for speed all pointing toward a monolith

blocks.content: 5.2 When it starts to genuinely hurt
blocks.text: 5.2 When it starts to genuinely hurt

blocks.content: ["Different parts of the app have wildly different scaling needs and that mismatch is now costing real money.","The team has grown large enough that deploys are constantly colliding and blocking each other.","One module's failures are regularly taking down unrelated features in production.","Domain boundaries have become clear and stable, and splitting would actually simplify ownership."]
items: Different parts of the app have wildly different scaling needs and that mismatch is now costing real money.
The team has grown large enough that deploys are constantly colliding and blocking each other.
One module's failures are regularly taking down unrelated features in production.
Domain boundaries have become clear and stable, and splitting would actually simplify ownership.

blocks.content: 5.3 Monolith first, split later

A common and healthy path is to start as a monolith, let the real module boundaries reveal themselves as the product matures, and only then consider peeling pieces off into separate services. Splitting too early, before you actually understand your domain, tends to produce worse boundaries than waiting would have.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396260802-27639581.png
blocks.alt: Starting as a monolith, learning real boundaries, then splitting only if needed

blocks.content: 6. Worked example: an e-commerce monolith

Picture a small e-commerce app with three obvious pieces, a catalog of products, a shopping cart, and order processing. As a monolith, all three live in one codebase, build into one deployable, and share one database.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262049-420189365.png
blocks.alt: Catalog, cart, and orders modules sharing one process and one database

blocks.content: 6.1 A simple folder structure
Even without splitting into services, the code can and should stay organized. Here is a reasonable layout for that same e-commerce monolith, already leaning toward a modular monolith.

ecommerce-app/
  src/
    catalog/
      catalog.controller.js
      catalog.service.js
      catalog.model.js
    cart/
      cart.controller.js
      cart.service.js
      cart.model.js
    orders/
      orders.controller.js
      orders.service.js
      orders.model.js
    shared/
      db.js
    app.js
  package.json

blocks.content: 6.2 A checkout flow that stays in one process
blocks.text: 6.2 A checkout flow that stays in one process

blocks.content: When a user checks out, the orders module needs the cart contents and needs to update product stock in catalog. In a monolith, that is just a couple of function calls, all inside one transaction.

blocks.title: One transaction, one commit or one rollback
blocks.content: Because all three modules share the same database connection here, this whole flow can be wrapped in a single database transaction. If reducing stock fails, the order creation can roll back too. That kind of consistency is genuinely hard to get across separate services.
7. The interview angle

A common trap in system design interviews is reaching for microservices immediately, as if that is automatically the sophisticated answer. It usually is not. Saying "I would start with a monolith" and explaining why is often the answer that signals real experience.

["State the trade-off explicitly, monoliths are simple and fast to ship but scale and fail as one unit.","Justify starting with a monolith for an early stage or small team product, and say what would change your mind later.","Mention the modular monolith as a way to get organization without paying for network calls you do not need yet.","If your interviewer pushes on scale, describe exactly which part would need to peel off first, and why, based on real bottlenecks."]
items: State the trade-off explicitly, monoliths are simple and fast to ship but scale and fail as one unit.
Justify starting with a monolith for an early stage or small team product, and say what would change your mind later.
Mention the modular monolith as a way to get organization without paying for network calls you do not need yet.
If your interviewer pushes on scale, describe exactly which part would need to peel off first, and why, based on real bottlenecks.

blocks.content: Monolith first is not the lazy answer. It is often the correct one, and knowing why is what separates experience from habit.
8. Key takeaways

["A monolith is one codebase, one build, one deploy, and usually one shared database, defined by deployment, not code quality.","It buys real simplicity: no network calls between your own modules, straightforward transactions, and easy debugging.","The real costs show up at scale: the whole app scales together, one team can break another's feature, deploys get riskier, and a crash in one module can take everything down.","A modular monolith keeps one deployable unit but organizes code into modules with clear boundaries, a strong middle ground.","Most startups, small teams, and products with unclear domain boundaries are better off starting as a monolith.","In interviews, do not reflexively reach for microservices, monolith first is a legitimate and often correct starting answer."]
items: A monolith is one codebase, one build, one deploy, and usually one shared database, defined by deployment, not code quality.
It buys real simplicity: no network calls between your own modules, straightforward transactions, and easy debugging.
The real costs show up at scale: the whole app scales together, one team can break another's feature, deploys get riskier, and a crash in one module can take everything down.
A modular monolith keeps one deployable unit but organizes code into modules with clear boundaries, a strong middle ground.
Most startups, small teams, and products with unclear domain boundaries are better off starting as a monolith.
In interviews, do not reflexively reach for microservices, monolith first is a legitimate and often correct starting answer.
